transcript.content: Hello, welcome. Can you tell me what’s been bringing you in today?

Well… I suppose what finally got me to make the appointment is that my concentration’s gotten a bit unreliable. I’m still managing, I think, but I’ll be reviewing a chart at the clinic, or even doing something quiet like laying out a watercolor wash, and then I realize I’ve read the same line three times. My mind has wandered off to everything that could go wrong. I don’t know if that’s the sort of thing you mean, but it’s been happening enough that I thought I should ask about it.
Do you find yourself worrying more than usual about things like work, health, or other everyday concerns, even when there isn’t a clear reason to be worried?

Yes… I think so. I mean, I try not to make too much of it, because everyone worries, don’t they? But my mind does keep circling around things—whether my old patients are being looked after properly, whether the handoff of the practice was financially sound, whether I’m going to become sort of… useless once I’m fully retired. 

Even saying it out loud, it sounds a bit much. The worries feel bigger than the actual problems, if that makes sense.
Have you noticed any physical symptoms, like restlessness, feeling on edge, or muscle tension, when these worries come up?

I’m not sure I’ve paid close enough attention to that, to be honest. I wouldn’t want to overstate it. I do sometimes feel… keyed up, maybe, when I’m worrying, but I haven’t really sorted out whether that’s physical or just me thinking too much. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
When you say you sometimes feel keyed up when worrying, does that come with physical sensations like restlessness, muscle tension, or feeling unable to relax?

I’m not entirely sure, honestly. I can tell that I feel wound up, but I haven’t really separated it into, you know, “my shoulders are tense” or “I can’t sit still” in any clear way. I probably haven’t been paying enough attention to it.

I don’t want to say yes just to be agreeable if I’m not certain. Does that make sense?
Do you find it difficult to control or stop the worrying once it starts?

Yes… though I suppose I’d like to think I can talk myself out of it. I try to reason with myself, really—almost the way I would with a nervous patient—but it doesn’t always stick.

One concern leads to the next, and before I know it I’m checking emails again, or reviewing old notes, or asking the same question more than once when I probably should just leave it alone. I know that may sound a bit excessive, but in the moment it feels like I’m just trying to be responsible.
Have you been feeling down, depressed, or losing interest or pleasure in activities you usually enjoy, even things like painting or other hobbies?

I don’t think so… not in any clear way. I mean, everyone has off days, and I’m not as energetic as I used to be, but I wouldn’t want to call it depression if that’s not really what it is.

With things like painting, I maybe don’t get to it as much as I should, but I haven’t really thought of it as losing interest. It’s more that other things get in the way, I suppose. Does that answer what you’re asking?
Have you been feeling fatigued or lacking in energy most days, even when you haven’t been doing anything particularly taxing?

A bit, yes. I don’t want to overstate it, because I can still get through the day, but by midafternoon I often feel pretty worn out.

It’s not always because I’ve done something strenuous, either. Even after a quiet morning, I can feel like a nap doesn’t really reset me. Simple things like weeding the garden or standing at the easel just feel heavier than they used to, if that makes sense.
Have you been having trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or waking up too early, even when you’re tired?

Yes… I suppose I have, though I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is.

Most nights I get into bed feeling tired, and then once everything is quiet, my mind starts going over things—patient transfers, little money details, whether I handled something properly. And even when I do fall asleep, I’m often awake around four or five, just lying there, feeling like I never quite settled.

I’m not sure if that’s the kind of sleep trouble you mean.
Have you noticed yourself feeling more irritable or easily annoyed, especially when you're worrying or feeling keyed up?

I’m not sure I’d say irritable, exactly. I mean, I try not to take things out on people, and I don’t think anyone would describe me as short-tempered.

Maybe I get a little tense or impatient when I’ve got something on my mind, but I usually keep it to myself. So… I haven’t really noticed being easily annoyed in a major way. Is that the sort of thing you mean?
Have you ever experienced sudden episodes where you feel intense fear or discomfort that comes on quickly and reaches a peak within minutes, like a panic attack?

No, I don’t think so. I mean, I’ve certainly felt anxious or keyed up at times, but not in that sudden, overwhelming way where it peaks within minutes.

I don’t believe I’ve had what people would call a panic attack. At least, not that I’m aware of.
Do you find that your anxiety or worry is not limited to specific situations, but rather occurs across a range of everyday events or activities, like work, health, or even small daily decisions?

Yes… I think that’s fair to say. It’s not just one particular thing, though I wish it were.

My mind tends to circle around all sorts of things—whether my old patients are being looked after properly, whether the handoff of the practice is financially sound, even whether I’ll become sort of… useless, I suppose, once I’m fully retired.

And I know some of that sounds normal, but it feels out of proportion even to me sometimes. Like I should be able to set it down, and I can’t quite manage it. Does that answer what you mean?
Have you found that things you used to enjoy, like painting or spending time with friends, don’t give you as much pleasure as they used to, even when you’re not particularly worried about anything?

I don’t think so, not really. I still enjoy things when I actually get myself to do them.

Maybe I’m a little less… enthusiastic at times, but I wouldn’t say the pleasure is gone. If I see friends or get absorbed in something, it can still feel good. I suppose I just don’t always make the effort as readily as I used to, but I’m not sure that’s the same thing.

Is that what you’re asking?
Do you find it harder than usual to make decisions or stay focused on tasks, even simple ones, because your mind keeps drifting to worries or other thoughts?

Yes… I’m afraid that has been happening more than I’d like to admit.

It’s not that I can’t think, exactly, but my concentration has become a bit unreliable. I’ll be reviewing a chart at the clinic, or even doing something pleasant like laying out a watercolor wash, and suddenly I realize I’ve read the same line three times—or I’ve stopped paying attention—because my mind has wandered off to everything that could go wrong.

I suppose that’s actually one of the main reasons I thought I should come in. I don’t want to overstate it, but it’s been noticeable.
Have you had days where you feel down or hopeless most of the time, even when there isn’t a clear reason for it?

Not most of the time, no. I mean, I have low moments, certainly—especially if I’ve been thinking too much—but I wouldn’t say I’m spending whole days feeling hopeless for no clear reason.

I don’t want to sound like I’m brushing it off, but it feels more like worry wearing me down than a constant sadness, if that makes sense.
Would you say that you feel anxious or worried on most days, even when there isn’t an immediate reason for concern?

Yes… I think I would have to say most days, yes.

I don’t mean I’m in a panic all the time or anything dramatic like that, but my mind keeps circling around things. Whether my old patients are being looked after properly, whether the handoff of the practice was really financially sound, whether I’m going to become… I don’t know, sort of useless once I’m fully retired.

And the thing is, even I can see it’s probably out of proportion. There isn’t always some immediate problem in front of me. It’s just that my mind seems to go looking for one. Does that make sense?
